The big problem with global warming isn't it making it too hot to live in areas. We could live in much hotter temperatures without even having to adapt much. The big problems are the secondary effects of the warming. The most obvious one is sea level change. Right now if all glacial ice melted it'd result in a sea level rise of about 230 feet. Humans tend to settle densely by the coasts and these areas would be deep underwater. We're even seeing a bit of this today as Florida is spending hundreds of millions of dollars on complex pumping systems to combat rising 'king tides' that are now starting to flood cities, roads, sewage systems, and pretty much anything near sea level. This article from the Miami Herald has some fun pics and stories. Crazy stuff.

Another problem is that the ocean is one of the biggest regulating systems of CO2 we have. It absorbs massive amounts of CO2 and converts it into carbonic acid. When our CO2 levels were in equilibrium this wasn't much of a problem, but now that CO2 levels are starting to get kind of crazy it's resulting in a gradual acidification of the ocean. Again, this doesn't mean you're going to step into the ocean and your bones melt. What it does do however is seriously damage small oceanic organisms from plankton to clams to coral. That in turn seriously damages the creatures that rely on those life to sustain themselves and so on all the way back up to us. Another issue there is that as the ocean becomes increasingly acidified it will work as less and less of a regulator of CO2 which will create one of the many feedback systems we have. The more you put in it, above equilibrium, the less it can store handle.

And there are lots of other little 'side effects' that will similarly affect us. Another example being increasing intensity of weather systems - for instance 2015 was the first time in recorded history there were 3 category 4 hurricanes in the Pacific simultaneously. But yeah, it's not like it's going to become so hot we all just shrivel up and die. It'll be a long, slow process. Which in some ways is maybe even worse. We're the allegorical frog in a pot of slowly boiling water. Feels pretty comfy!

I see. Wouldn't one of the side effects of raised CO2 levels be increased growth of plants ? Ie. those plants that live off of CO2 would grow more - consuming more CO2 ? Looking at recent history, Genghis Khan's approach of killing off half the people who burned trees and coal for warmth caused exactly that. Lowering of CO2 because more trees.

Whatever effect this would have is something we're already experiencing today. This, like I mentioned with the boiling frog allegory, is the really insidious part about all of this. It's not like there's some point in time where all these things just suddenly go from 0 to 1. Everything I've described is already happening today and so to is any positive dampening affect from an increase in plant growth.

The short answer is yes, but there are other problems. Yes on the average places are getting warmer, however the peaks are getting higher as well. Meaning inclement weather in summer and in winter get to more intense extremes. Going to somewhere like Alaska, Greenland, or parts of Russia, you will find the summers warmer, but you also might find the winter storms worse as well.
